exam: What is the most appropriate first investigation for a 6‑month‑old with a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border? — Echocardiography to assess gradient and anatomy.
A child with PS presents with syncope during play. What is the most likely underlying mechanism? — Severe RV outflow obstruction leading to transient cerebral hypoperfusion.
You have a 10‑year‑old with PS and a VSD. Which intervention is preferred if the PS gradient is 45 mmHg? — Balloon valvuloplasty before addressing the VSD.
Why is a loud harsh murmur at the left upper sternal border characteristic of PS? — It reflects high‑velocity jet across a narrowed pulmonary valve.
A patient with PS is admitted with dehydration. What is the immediate priority? — Rehydrate to prevent worsening RV failure.
Which drug is contraindicated in PS due to risk of worsening obstruction? — Calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil) because they reduce RV contractility.
How would you differentiate PS from aortic stenosis on auscultation? — PS murmur is left upper sternal border; aortic stenosis is right upper sternal border.
What is the key echocardiographic sign of severe PS? — Peak systolic gradient >50 mmHg with RV hypertrophy.

sections.p: Pulmonary stenosis (PS) is a congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract that impedes systolic blood flow into the pulmonary artery.
